newsitem.title: EGYPT: Turkey says Israel link commercial, not alliance.
newsitem.headline: Turkey says Israel link commercial, not alliance.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan said on Thursday a military agreement between his country and Israel was not an alliance but a commercial deal "like buying a kilo of apples in the market."
Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, accused the Jewish state of jeopardising Middle East peace with its treatment of Palestinians.
He spoke to reporters after talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Prime Minister Kamal el-Ganzouri at the start of trip that is to include Libya, despite U.S. opposition.

"We have to put in perspective what is the nature of the cooperation with Israel. We have a category of aircraft which is equipped with sophisticated devices. They cannot be maintained or overhauled by Turkish technicians. With this contract we are going to get the know-how," Erbakan said.

"Israel is the country where this could be done but this is a commercial deal... there is no difference between this and buying a kilo of apples in the market. A country like Turkey, which has such strong relations with the Islamic world, cannot go on with Israel in such things as an alliance," he added.
Turkey and Israel have signed two deals this year that have angered Arab and Moslem countries.

An agreement in February allowing Israeli air force jets to train over Turkey drew protests from Turkish Islamists. Before taking power, Erbakan vowed to annul the agreement but he has since abandoned any action.
In August, Turkey and Israel signed a defence industry cooperation deal.
Turkish President Suleyman Demirel said last month the pacts with Israel remained despite the new Islamist-led government but emphasised that neither accord was directed against a third country.

Erbakan's spokesman said Turkey urged Israel to reconsider its decision to open a new entrance to a tunnel near Jerusalem's al-Aqsa mosque, the third holiest site in Islam. The opening sparked clashes between Palestinians and Israeli troops in which 73 people were killed.
"The other side (Israel) must stop the behaviour and the provocations that harm the peace process," said government spokesman Abdullah Gul.
Erbakan was pessimistic about the U.S.-organised summit in Washington that ended on Wednesday and had aimed to ease tension between Palestinians and Israelis.

"We are saddened that the summit did not come up with the required results. This behaviour and provocations that are aimed at harming the peace process are totally rejected by the Islamic world and Moslems in particular," Erbakan said.
Erbakan arrived in Cairo on Wednesday ahead of a controversial trip to Libya and Nigeria that has renewed concern that he aims to divert Turkey away from the West.
Gul brushed aside criticism by Washington and Erbakan's secular coalition partners of the trip to Libya, which Washington says is a sponsor of political violence.
"Turkey is an independent country that has the powers and perogatives to make a decision. We have diplomatic relations with Libya and it is natural that we have commerial ties with Libya," Gul said.
Turkish officials have already arrived in Tripoli to seek payment of outstanding debts of up to $365 million owed to Turkish building contractors.
